title: Strat Chat - Underrated Checks for Understanding
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: This Strat Chat installment explores two underused checking-for-understanding strategies that go beyond the standard repertoire of true/false, multiple choice, and think/pair/share. The author argues that while classic CFU techniques are valuable, over-reliance on a predictable rotation can cause students to run on autopilot without generating the cognitive friction needed for durable learning. The first strategy, 'Tell me why ___ is incorrect,' inverts the standard MCQ or true/false check by asking students to explain wrong answers rather than identify right ones—forcing students to engage with the logic behind distractors and expose misconceptions. The second, 'You Be The Assessor,' gives students a sample answer to evaluate and score, requiring them to understand not just what is correct but what makes an answer excellent or incomplete. Both strategies demand deeper reasoning than simply selecting a correct response, and both can be enhanced by AI-generated plausible-but-wrong responses. The author frames these techniques as tools for varying the texture of instruction and preventing the habitual responses that undermine meaningful formative assessment.
points: Overusing any single CFU technique causes students to shift from active thinking to autopilot—rotating strategies keeps the cognitive friction high and supports durable learning.
'Tell me why ___ is incorrect' triples response opportunities in a single MCQ by asking students to explain each distractor, turning a low-stakes question into a high-inference reasoning task.
'You Be The Assessor' requires students to apply their knowledge to evaluate and score a sample answer, which demands understanding of how content is applied—not just what the content is.
Incorporating common misconceptions into 'You Be The Assessor' sample answers creates targeted opportunities to catch and correct those misconceptions before they solidify.
AI tools can generate intelligent-sounding wrong answers efficiently, making the creation of 'You Be The Assessor' materials faster and more targeted than manual construction.
quotes: There's no denying, Checking for Understanding is the greatest tool a teacher has to inform them of current student performance and misconceptions developing at a whole class level. It is an avenue to create a positive feedback loop with students while also creating formative action to correct and improve upon misconceptions or incomplete responses.

The best teachers will not only check for understanding, they will have a repertoire of a small and powerful set of strategies and change the way in which they check regularly to keep things fresh for the students as well as varying whether they are required to think fast or think slow.

We can however fall into a trap that our lessons will become rigid and formulaic where students are hit with content, true/false, content, MCQ, content, think/pair/share in such a consistent order that students move from active engagement in the thinking to running on autopilot.

We know the use of examples and non-examples is a useful tool in explicit teaching and a similar logic applies here. If students understand what the answer is, we also need them to understand what the answer isn't.
Suddenly, this scenario has gone from Adam having a 50/50 chance at being correct to needing to explain his thinking in more depth.

AI tools can also be your friend in the creation of these imperfect responses as our LLM friends are able to punch out intelligent sounding nonsense both deliberately and accidentally which can be of great use for our classes.
